turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry we're late, the ring road was a nightmare and then we couldn't find a space in the car park.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're alright, we were running a bit behind ourselves. Come and sit down.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I did say leave earlier. A lorry had shed its load by the roundabout, pallets all over the lane.
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): And the wipers gave up in that drizzle, which was the last thing we needed. Anyway, we're here.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. The nurse grabbed your observations on the way in.
[SEG0006] person_4 (NURSE): Mm. Blood pressure one thirty two over eighty four, pulse 78, temperature 36.9, oxygen sats 98 percent. All sitting nicely.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks. So what brings you in?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm, it's my nose. It's completely bunged up, there's this thick green stuff coming out, and my face feels like someone's squeezing it.
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): I keep thinking if I blow hard enough it'll clear, but it just makes my ears pop and nothing useful comes out except more of that green muck.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has the blockage and the green discharge been there?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Ten days. I counted on the kitchen calendar because I knew you'd want a number. The cold started before that, about a fortnight ago.
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): The sore throat from the cold has gone, that was the first few days, scratchy and then it just faded. I was drinking honey and lemon like my mother used to.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the pressure in the face, is that the same ten days?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, both cheeks, just under the eyes. It's a dull ache, and it gets worse when I bend down to tie my shoes or pick up the post.
[SEG0015] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's been absolutely shattered with it as well.
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, the tiredness. It's the second week of that now, so two weeks of feeling wiped out. I'm on the sofa by half seven and I usually last till eleven.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or have you felt hot and shivery at all?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No. I've been using the little digital thermometer at home, morning and evening, and it's been normal every single time. No shivers, no sweats.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or trouble getting your breath?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No cough now. There was a cold cough at the start but it went after a few days. Breathing is fine, I did two flights of stairs this morning and I wasn't gasping.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any change in your vision, or double vision?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): No, the eyes are fine. I had new glasses in the spring but that's just because the old ones were scratched, nothing to do with this.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Toothache, or pain in the top teeth?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): No, teeth are alright. Dentist in June said everything was sound, no fillings even.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any swelling of the face that you've noticed, or a rash?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): No swelling and no rash. I checked in the bathroom mirror this morning, both sides look the same as ever.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): What have you actually been putting in the nose?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Otrivene, the decongestant spray, the one from Boots. Two squirts each side, morning and night, every day for these ten days.

[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): The box says don't use it more than a week, I know, the chemist even pointed at the leaflet, but it was the only thing that let me sleep so I carried on. I also take two paracetamol when the face is really bad, not every day.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any antihistamine, or anything else from the surgery?

[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): I was on fexofenadyne, a hundred and eighty milligrams, one tablet a day by mouth, for the hay fever. I stopped it in March when the pollen dropped off. They mentioned a steroid nose spray once but I never collected it from the chemist.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, penicillin in particular?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. I had penicillin as a child for my tonsils and I was absolutely fine with it.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is the hay fever still an ongoing thing for you?

[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh yes, I've had hay fever since my twenties. Every summer I get itchy eyes and a runny nose, that's why I was on the fexofenadyne. It's quieter now we're into autumn, it never fully leaves but it's not what I'm here for.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, so the hay fever sits in the background. Do you smoke?

[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Never. My brother smokes like a chimney but I never started. I work in the council archives, fifteen years now, and it's dusty down there, paper dust, which I suppose doesn't help a nose.

[SEG0038] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Dusty is one word for it. Speaking of being stuck indoors, did you catch the test match on Sunday? England were absolutely hopeless, and then the rain came and we just sat there with the tea going cold.

[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Don't start him on the cricket, doctor, we'll be here till next week. He rewound the highlights three times. The weather was grim though, that drizzle followed us all the way from the ring road.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha, I'll leave the cricket. Let me have a look in the nose while we're here.

[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Lining of both nostrils looks swollen, and there's green mucus sitting in the right one. Both cheeks are tender when I press. Throat's clear, ears look fine, and I can't see any swelling of the face.

[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, thinking it through, this fits an acute sinusitis coming off the back of that cold. Most of these are viral, and the green colour on its own doesn't prove bacteria. The majority settle over two or three weeks without an antibiotic.

[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): My neighbour had something like this and they gave her antibiotics on day three and she swore by them. I don't want to be difficult, I just don't want it going into my ears or something.

[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're not being difficult. I'm not starting an antibiotic today, because the guidelines and, frankly, the lack of fever are against it. What I will do is a back-up prescription.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Amoxicillin, five hundred milligrams, three times a day, for five days, by mouth. Don't start it now. Only start it if you're no better in a week, or if you get a fever.

[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): And the spray, do I keep going with the otrivene? Because if I skip the morning dose I'm bunged up by lunch and then I can't taste my sandwich, which sounds silly but it's miserable.

[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stop the otrivene. After ten days it starts to cause its own blockage, a rebound thing, so carrying on is probably feeding the problem. Saline rinses, the salt-water ones, a couple of times a day, and carry on with the paracetamol when the face aches.

[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): Saline, right. Err, I tried a salt thing once years ago and it went down the back of my throat and I coughed it across the kitchen, so I'll go gently. Will the amoxacillin upset my stomach? I have a work thing on Thursday.

[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take it with food if you do start it, and stop and ring us if you get a rash or bad diarrhoea. Most people are fine. Thursday you'll still be on the saline and paracetamol, not the antibiotic, unless you've suddenly got a fever.
[SEG0050] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll make sure he doesn't start the capsules early. He likes to get ahead of things.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you're no better in a week, or you're worsening before that, come back and see me. Otherwise you don't need a routine appointment.
[SEG0052] person_1 (PATIENT): That's clear, thank you. Sorry again about the parking, the machine ate my pound coin on the way in, which felt personal.
[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): These machines have it in for everyone. Collect the back-up script at reception on your way out, and we'll leave it there.

spec.situation: Blocked nose, facial pressure and green discharge ten days after a cold; second week of tiredness; uses nasal spray daily; doctor explains most settle without antibiotics, gives a back-up plan.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

bad.reason: Only medicine allergies were discussed; no general allergy denial stated.
